case_facts: My landlord is trying to evict me from my flat with 3 days notice though I've paid rent on time for 5 years.

analysis.summary: A tenant who has consistently paid rent on time for five years is facing eviction by their landlord with only three days' notice. The tenant disputes the eviction as unlawful given the absence of any default or valid ground for eviction. The core dispute concerns the adequacy of notice and the legality of the eviction proceedings.

issues.issue: Adequacy of notice period: whether 3 days' notice is legally sufficient to terminate a long-standing tenancy
Grounds for eviction: whether a landlord can evict a tenant who has paid rent regularly and on time without establishing a valid statutory ground
issues.governing_law: State Rent Control Act / Transfer of Property Act 1882

issues.issue: Tenant's right to protection against arbitrary eviction under applicable Rent Control legislation
issues.governing_law: State Rent Control Act (e.g., Delhi Rent Control Act 1958 / Model Tenancy Act 2021)

issues.issue: Whether the eviction notice is void ab initio for non-compliance with mandatory procedural requirements
issues.governing_law: Section 106, Transfer of Property Act 1882; Code of Civil Procedure 1908

transcript.speaker: ai
transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I appear on behalf of the Plaintiff, a tenant of five years of unblemished standing, who now faces the unconscionable threat of being thrown onto the street with a mere three days' notice. I submit that this eviction attempt is not merely a contractual dispute — it strikes at the very heart of constitutional protections that this Hon'ble Court is duty-bound to uphold.

Your Lordship, the foundational pillar of my case rests upon the landmark judgment of this very Supreme Court in **Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation** (docid: 3004510). That judgment unequivocally recognised that the right to livelihood is an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. Critically, the Court held that even where a party's occupation of premises may be questioned, the procedure for eviction must be **fair and reasonable**, and reasonable notice together with an opportunity to be heard must be afforded before any eviction is carried out. My client is not an encroacher — she is a law-abiding tenant who has paid every rupee of rent punctually for five consecutive years. If even encroachers are entitled to reasonable notice and a hearing, it is inconceivable that a bona fide tenant of five years can be dispossessed in three days without any due process whatsoever.

Your Lordship, three days' notice is not "reasonable notice" by any stretch of legal imagination. My client's home is her shelter, her sanctuary, and the base from which she earns her livelihood. To uproot her overnight, without cause, without adequate notice, and without any opportunity to be heard, is to strike at her right to life itself. The Defendant-landlord has offered no justification — no breach of tenancy terms, no arrears, no statutory ground — nothing. This is naked, arbitrary exercise of power, and this Court has consistently held that arbitrariness is the antithesis of the rule of law.

I therefore urge Your Lordship to grant immediate interim relief restraining the Defendant from proceeding with this eviction, and to ultimately declare the three-day notice void ab initio as being in violation of the principles of natural justice and the constitutional guarantee under Article 21. The facts are stark, the law is clear, and justice demands nothing less.
